title: Ask about the light, not the caste
hook: recognize the light in everyone and do not ask their caste (Asa, ang 349)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhand, woman, and Guru Nanak's question; your line was why call her lesser. Today, another label the Gurus refused to use.

Where are you from? What do you do? Where did you go to school? What's your last name? Those questions can be friendly. They can also be a way of sorting, placing someone on a ladder before you know them at all. In Guru Nanak's world, the big sorting question was caste, the group you were born into, which could decide whom you ate with and whom you married. Guru Nanak had a one-line answer: ask about the light.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU FROM? WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `QUESTIONS THAT SORT.` → `THE BIG QUESTION THEN: CASTE.`

segments.voice: On Ang 349, in Rag Asa, Guru Nanak sings: jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee aagai jaat na he. Recognize the light, don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. Jot is light, the divine light Sikhs believe shines in every person. Jaat is caste, birth-group. And the verbs are the point: jaanahu, know, recognize; na poochhahu, don't even ask. Guru Nanak isn't only saying caste doesn't matter to God. He's saying don't make it the first question you put to a human being. The Gurus didn't leave this as a nice sentence. They built it into furniture and food. In the langar, the free kitchen, everyone sits on the floor in the same rows, the pangat, and eats the same meal, whoever they are. Tradition tells that Guru Amar Das asked visitors, even the Mughal emperor Akbar, to eat in the langar before meeting him. Later, tradition says, when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, the five who first stepped forward came from different castes and regions, and they drank amrit from one bowl. Caste didn't vanish from Punjabi life, Sikh life included, and the line still challenges the communities that sing it. But the rule on paper is clear, and it's short. Before you ask what someone's label is, see what's shining in them.
screen: `JOT — THE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · `JAAT — DON'T EVEN ASK.` · `ONE ROW, ONE MEAL: THE PANGAT.` · `FIVE BACKGROUNDS, ONE BOWL.` · then, large: `SEE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you usually file under a label, the new hire, the neighbor, the person at the counter, the relative you've decided about, and set the label down, the way you'd set down a bag. Look at them again in your mind: a face, a life, a light. Breathe in and silently say, see the light; breathe out, and stay here a while.
Jot, light, the divine light in every person. Guru Nanak's line in Asa: recognize it, and don't ask their caste.
Your line: see the light. One row, one meal, one bowl. See you next time.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara langar, people of any background sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor and eat the same free meal; Sikh teaching rejects caste distinctions, though caste still shapes parts of community life.

original.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light; jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee, recognize the light, don't ask the caste.

trapdoor: what you thought: caste just doesn't matter to God.
what it means: don't make someone's label the first thing you ask; recognize the light in them first.
what a scholar hears: Asa Mahala 1, Ang 349; jot (light) set against jaat (birth-group), with the imperative na poochhahu; the langar's pangat made the teaching physical.
